questions.prompt: A client calls a tool named archive_invoice on a server that never defined it, and receives {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":9,"error":{"code":-32602,"message":"Unknown tool: archive_invoice"}}. What does this exchange illustrate about how MCP standardizes integrations?
options: Every MCP server must implement the exact same tool names so clients never see this error
Each server defines its own tool surface, and clients discover it rather than assuming a shared fixed catalog
Unknown tool names sent by any client are always silently ignored by the server rather than being returned as an explicit error
The client should have used method notifications/tools/list_changed to avoid this particular error entirely
questions.explanation: MCP does not standardize which tools exist, only how a client asks what tools exist and how it calls them, so a server is free to not implement a given tool and the client must discover the real surface through tools/list rather than assuming a universal catalog. That is what keeps the protocol generic across unrelated systems.

questions.objective: Distinguish the responsibilities of MCP hosts, clients, and servers and how discovery and capability negotiation connect them
questions.prompt: A host connects to two servers whose discover results both carry "_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo":{"name":"files","version":"1.0.0"}}. How should the host key its routing table for these two connections?
options: By serverInfo.version, since the version string separates servers that share a name
By whichever server answered discovery first, since later duplicates must be dropped
By an identifier the host assigns to each connection, since serverInfo is self-reported
By serverInfo.name, since the specification guarantees that server names are unique
questions.explanation: serverInfo is self-reported display and logging metadata, so two unrelated servers can report the same name and version. The host owns its connections and should route by an identifier it assigns to each one, never by a value a server chose for itself.

questions.objective: Read the schemas and structured data that define MCP messages, tool definitions, capabilities, and server manifests
questions.prompt: A server answers server/discover with {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"result":{"resultType":"complete","instructions":"Use tools for weather lookups."}}. What is missing from this DiscoverResult?
options: A cursor field so the client can request the next page of capabilities
A serverInfo object nested directly under result rather than under result._meta
An inputRequests map describing which elicitation request the server needs answered first
The supportedVersions and capabilities fields, plus the ttlMs and cacheScope caching fields
questions.explanation: DiscoverResult is defined as a cacheable result that must carry supportedVersions and capabilities as its core content, along with ttlMs and cacheScope because server/discover is one of the operations whose complete result must include caching hints. None of those required fields appear in this response.

questions.objective: Distinguish the responsibilities of MCP hosts, clients, and servers and how discovery and capability negotiation connect them
questions.prompt: A server rejects a tools/call with {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":21,"error":{"code":-32021,"message":"Missing required client capability"}}. Why is this error response incomplete?
options: It needs data.requiredCapabilities, naming what the client must declare to succeed
It needs resultType set to input_required so the client can answer the capability question
It needs data.supported, listing the protocol versions that the server accepts
It needs an HTTP 404 status, since a missing capability means the method is unknown
questions.explanation: MissingRequiredClientCapability tells the client exactly what to add: its data carries requiredCapabilities, the capabilities the client must declare when it retries. data.supported belongs to UnsupportedProtocolVersionError, the HTTP status for this error is 400 rather than 404, and an error response never carries a resultType.

questions.objective: Read the schemas and structured data that define MCP messages, tool definitions, capabilities, and server manifests
questions.prompt: A tool definition includes "inputSchema": {"properties": {}}, with no type keyword at the root. What must be corrected for this to be a valid MCP tool definition?
options: The properties field must be renamed to arguments to match the tools/call request shape
The root of inputSchema must declare type object, since tool arguments are always a JSON object
An outputSchema must always be declared whenever an inputSchema is present on a tool
The schema must also set additionalProperties to true so that any unknown extra arguments are silently accepted
questions.explanation: Tool arguments are always JSON objects, so the specification requires type object at the root of inputSchema even though most other JSON Schema 2020-12 keywords are optional and flexible. Without that root type declaration the schema does not describe a valid call shape for the tool.

questions.objective: Read the schemas and structured data that define MCP messages, tool definitions, capabilities, and server manifests
questions.prompt: A tool defines an outputSchema and its CallToolResult includes both content and structuredContent. Which two statements about this pattern are correct under MCP 2026-07-28? Select two.
options: structuredContent must always be a JSON object and can never be a plain string, number, or array
A tool without any outputSchema is not permitted to ever include a structuredContent field
The structuredContent should conform to the declared outputSchema and also be mirrored into a text block
Arguments that violate the tool's inputSchema come back as isError true rather than a protocol error
questions.explanation: structuredContent can be any JSON value, and when an outputSchema exists the server should make it conform while also serializing it into a text block for clients that only read content. Separately, schema violations in tool arguments are reported as a normal result with isError true so the model can see and correct them, not as a JSON-RPC error.

questions.objective: Read the schemas and structured data that define MCP messages, tool definitions, capabilities, and server manifests
questions.prompt: A reviewer reads a manifest entry for a tool named delete_record with no annotations block at all, whose result carries {"cacheScope":"public","ttlMs":60000} even though the data it returns is specific to one authenticated user. Which two observations belong in the review? Select two.
options: With no annotations present, the effective destructiveHint defaults to true, so this tool should be treated as capable of destructive changes
Because cacheScope is set to public here, the server has already enforced correct access control for this data
A public cacheScope on a result containing one user's private data risks that response being served to a different user
The missing annotations block means the server has violated the specification and the manifest must be rejected outright
questions.explanation: Tool annotations are optional hints with real defaults, so an absent annotations block still implies destructiveHint true, which a reviewer should flag rather than assume the tool is safe. Separately, cacheScope public is a sharing hint, not an access control, so pairing it with per-user data is a genuine risk regardless of how the response happens to be cached.

questions.objective: Trace the model interaction flow from a user request through the host, model, client, and server and back into model context
questions.prompt: A model calls a tool with a malformed date argument and the client receives back a CallToolResult with isError true and content explaining the expected date format. What happens next in the interaction flow?
options: The server closes the connection because an isError result always ends the current interaction
The client automatically retries the exact same arguments a second time without involving the model
The tool execution error is added to model context so the model can revise arguments and call again
The host discards the conversation and starts an entirely new request to the model from scratch
questions.explanation: Tool execution errors are deliberately returned as ordinary results with isError true precisely so their explanatory content re-enters model context, letting the model reason about what went wrong and issue a corrected tools/call. Discarding the conversation or blindly retrying identical arguments would both defeat that self-correction design.

questions.objective: Trace the model interaction flow from a user request through the host, model, client, and server and back into model context
questions.prompt: A host builds model context for a turn where the model will decide whether to call a tool. Which information actually becomes part of what the model sees?
options: The authorization server's private signing key used to validate the client's bearer token
The server's internal process id and the file system path where it is installed
The raw HTTP headers such as Mcp-Method that the client attached to the previous request
The tool's name, description, and input schema, plus the content of any prior results
questions.explanation: The model reasons only over what the host places in its context: tool names, descriptions, schemas, and the content of results including tool execution errors. Transport level headers, server process internals, and authorization secrets never belong in that context and must stay outside what the model can see.

questions.objective: Identify the protocol primitives and utilities, including tools, resources, prompts, completion, caching, pagination, transports, and deprecated client features
questions.prompt: A tool result includes this embedded resource content block on one line: {"type":"resource","resource":{"uri":"file:///report.txt","mimeType":"text/plain","text":"Q3 totals","annotations":{"audience":["user"]}}}. Where does the schema say annotations actually belongs on this content block?
options: Beside resource as a sibling field on the EmbeddedResource block itself, not nested inside it
Inside a separate _meta.annotations key rather than as a top level annotations field at all
Nested inside the resource object exactly as shown, since ResourceContents defines its own annotations field
Only on the outer CallToolResult, never on an individual embedded resource content block
questions.explanation: The schema defines EmbeddedResource with an annotations field alongside its resource field, while ResourceContents itself carries no annotations property. A tool result that nests annotations inside the resource object instead of placing it as a sibling field does not match the structure the schema actually defines.

questions.objective: Apply the request, notification, subscription, and multi round-trip interaction patterns and handle each result type
questions.prompt: Two different client connections to the same server, using the same authorization, call tools/list one after another with no tool changes in between. What must be true of the two ListToolsResult payloads?
options: They may list different tools because each connection is treated as an independent session
They must list the same set of tools, because tools/list must not vary per connection
They must each include a fresh resultType of input_required just to confirm that the underlying connection is still alive
They may omit ttlMs on the second call since the first call already cached the result
questions.explanation: Because MCP is stateless, tools/list results must not vary per connection or as a side effect of other requests, only possibly by the authorization presented on the request. With identical authorization and no server side change, two separate connections must see the same set of tools; returning them in a deterministic order is a SHOULD, and every complete result still carries its own ttlMs.

mock-03.title: MCPA Full-Length Mock 3: Design and Security Trade-offs

questions.objective: Describe the core MCP concepts of hosts, clients, servers, primitives, and the stateless JSON-RPC request model
questions.prompt: A team migrating to MCP 2026-07-28 complains that servers can no longer remember a shopping cart between calls the way a session used to. What does the stateless design actually require them to do instead, and why is that the right trade?
options: Mint a server handle for the cart, return it in a result, and have the client pass it back as an argument
Open one dedicated connection to a single replica so that replica can hold the cart in its own memory
Send an initialize request each morning so the server can attach the cart to that entire day's ongoing handshake process every time
Resend the entire cart's contents inside the JSON-RPC id field on every single request the client makes
questions.explanation: Statelessness means a server cannot rely on a prior request on the same connection, so any state that must span calls needs an explicit, server-minted, opaque handle passed back as a normal argument. That is what lets any replica answer any request, which is the whole payoff of dropping sessions.

questions.objective: Describe the core MCP concepts of hosts, clients, servers, primitives, and the stateless JSON-RPC request model
questions.prompt: A backend engineer proposes storing per-client state keyed by the underlying TCP connection so a server can skip re-reading arguments on every call. Why does this design break the 2026-07-28 statelessness guarantee even if it works in a single-server test?
options: It requires every client to install a new certificate before it can open any connection at all
It makes a call's outcome depend on which connection carried it, so no other replica can serve it correctly
It duplicates work that tools/list pagination already performs whenever a result set grows large across many separate paginated requests
It is disallowed only because TCP connections run slower than the stdio transport for local servers
questions.explanation: Connection-keyed state reintroduces exactly the stickiness that 2026-07-28 removed: a load balancer could route the next call to a different replica, or the client could reconnect, and the server would answer incorrectly. The fix is an explicit handle carried in the request, not implicit connection memory.

questions.objective: Read the MCP specification, its revision history, and its feature lifecycle to tell current, deprecated, and removed behavior apart
questions.prompt: A team debating how to pin its integration asks why MCP names revisions with dates such as 2026-07-28 instead of semantic version numbers. What does the date in a revision identifier signify?
options: The day every earlier revision stopped working, since each date retires older revisions
The day the revision's governance vote closed, whatever the revision happened to change
The last date backwards incompatible changes were made, so compatible updates keep it
The release date of the newest SDK that implements the revision's full feature set
questions.explanation: A protocol version string is a date in YYYY-MM-DD form marking the last date backwards incompatible changes were made; the specification can still receive backwards compatible updates without changing it. Older revisions do not stop working on that date, and SDK release dates or governance votes play no part in the identifier.

questions.objective: Reason about interoperability, protocol versioning, and the value of one open protocol over per-system custom integrations
questions.prompt: A company already has a proprietary message format tuned exactly to its internal tools and refuses to adopt MCP, arguing their format is simpler for their own use. What is the clearest cost of that choice as new AI hosts and external systems appear?
options: Their format will automatically gain OAuth 2.1 support the moment a new host adopts it
Nothing changes at all, since message formats never affect how many separate integrations a team must eventually build
Their proprietary format will be forced to add roots and sampling to remain usable
Every new host or system still needs a bespoke adapter instead of reusing a compliant client or server
questions.explanation: A protocol tailored to one shop's current tools does not become more useful as the ecosystem grows. Each new host or system still needs a custom adapter, which is exactly the integration cost that adopting a shared, versioned protocol like MCP was meant to remove.

questions.objective: Reason about interoperability, protocol versioning, and the value of one open protocol over per-system custom integrations
questions.prompt: Which two outcomes does adopting one open, versioned protocol provide that a set of per-system custom integrations does not? Select two.
options: Every tool call is guaranteed to complete in the same amount of time on any server
Every server automatically becomes free to operate no matter its own infrastructure costs
A revision timeline and feature lifecycle give teams a shared way to plan migrations together
A client built against the specification can work with servers it has never seen before
questions.explanation: Interoperability and a shared versioning and deprecation process are the concrete benefits of one open protocol. Cost and latency are operational properties of each deployment and are not guaranteed by the protocol itself, so they make weak justifications for standardization.

questions.objective: Read the MCP specification, its revision history, and its feature lifecycle to tell current, deprecated, and removed behavior apart
questions.prompt: A code reviewer flags a server that still implements roots/list and sampling/createMessage as inputRequests, calling it out of date for 2026-07-28. Is the reviewer's conclusion correct?
options: No, since roots and sampling are deprecated, not removed, and remain functional until a later revision removes them
Yes, since a deprecated feature can never legally be shipped inside any conformant 2026-07-28 production server deployment
No, since roots and sampling were never mentioned in any revision released before 2026-07-28
Yes, since any feature with a documented migration path must already be gone from the specification
questions.explanation: The feature lifecycle distinguishes deprecated from removed. Roots, sampling, and logging are deprecated in 2026-07-28 with a stated migration path, but they still work, with the earliest possible removal in the first revision released on or after 2027-07-28, so the server is not out of date.

questions.objective: Read the MCP specification, its revision history, and its feature lifecycle to tell current, deprecated, and removed behavior apart
questions.prompt: A governance team assumes every deprecated MCP feature shares the same earliest removal floor as roots and sampling, the first revision on or after 2027-07-28. Why is applying that same floor to the HTTP+SSE transport a mistake?
options: It is not a mistake at all, since every feature deprecated by any means shares exactly one single common removal floor
HTTP+SSE was deprecated earlier in 2025-03-26 by a different SEP, with its own floor tied to that SEP reaching Final
The floor only ever applies to purely client-side features in general, and HTTP+SSE simply counts as a server-side transport feature instead
HTTP+SSE cannot be deprecated at all, since transports are explicitly exempt from the feature lifecycle policy
questions.explanation: Each deprecated feature carries its own origin and removal floor rather than one shared date. Roots, sampling, logging, and Dynamic Client Registration were deprecated in 2026-07-28 with an earliest removal on or after 2027-07-28, but HTTP+SSE was deprecated back in 2025-03-26, so its floor runs from that earlier SEP reaching Final instead.

questions.objective: Describe the core MCP concepts of hosts, clients, servers, primitives, and the stateless JSON-RPC request model
questions.prompt: A skeptical architect asks why MCP does not simply negotiate protocol version and capabilities once, the way many handshake-based protocols do, instead of repeating them on every request. What is the accurate 2026-07-28 rationale?
options: Negotiating once is impossible in JSON-RPC, which has no concept of a request at all
The specification requires it only so that gateways have more spare bytes available for careful rate limiting decisions
Repeating metadata on every request lets any request be handled correctly without depending on what happened earlier
It only matters for HTTP transports, since stdio connections keep negotiated state in memory regardless
questions.explanation: Per-request metadata is a direct consequence of statelessness: a server must not infer version or capabilities from earlier requests on the same connection. That is what allows requests to be retried or rerouted to a different replica safely, on stdio and HTTP alike.

questions.objective: Explain the purpose and scope of MCP and the integration problem it standardizes between AI applications and external systems
questions.prompt: Select the three things MCP deliberately leaves for the host, the model provider, or the external system to decide, rather than standardizing itself.
options: How a host's user interface presents a conversation to a person
The shape of a JSON-RPC request, result, error, and notification message
Which large language model the host uses to reason about a request
The internal business logic that a connected external system runs
questions.explanation: MCP standardizes the wire format connecting applications and external systems, not the model choice, the host UI, or what a system does internally. The JSON-RPC message shapes are exactly the part the protocol does define, which is why it is the one item outside the deliberately unstandardized set.

questions.objective: Read the MCP specification, its revision history, and its feature lifecycle to tell current, deprecated, and removed behavior apart
questions.prompt: While researching a fine point of client registration, an engineer finds an open SEP pull request proposing a shorter tool name format, and separately the published specification page that already documents a different, current format. Which should the engineer treat as authoritative for a 2026-07-28 deployment?
options: Whichever document was edited more recently in the source repository's commit history
Neither, since naming rules are left entirely to each individual server implementation to freely decide upon
The SEP pull request, since proposals always describe where the specification is heading next
The published specification page, since a draft proposal is not yet part of the current revision
questions.explanation: Reading the specification means treating the published, current revision as the source of truth and a draft SEP as, at most, a preview of a possible future change. Until a proposal is accepted and released, the specification page's rule is what a 2026-07-28 implementation must follow.

questions.objective: Distinguish the responsibilities of MCP hosts, clients, and servers and how discovery and capability negotiation connect them
questions.prompt: A host developer proposes sharing a single client instance across three different MCP servers to save memory, routing all three connections' messages through it. What is the strongest reason MCP hosts instead embed one client per server connection?
options: Each server connection has its own capabilities and cache, and mixing them in one client would blur which server a message belongs to
Sharing a client this way would also clearly violate the important rule that tools must always stay strictly model-controlled rather than application-driven
Servers absolutely refuse to respond at all unless exactly one single dedicated TCP port stays wide open on the host machine itself
A shared client is forbidden since JSON-RPC ids must stay globally unique across an entire operating system
questions.explanation: A client's job is to hold one server's negotiated capabilities, discovery results, and cache state cleanly. Merging three servers behind one client risks attributing a result, a capability, or a cached entry to the wrong server, which the one-client-per-server design avoids by construction.

questions.objective: Distinguish the responsibilities of MCP hosts, clients, and servers and how discovery and capability negotiation connect them
questions.prompt: A gateway aggregates two independent servers that both expose a tool named search. What is the correct design for the aggregated tool registry the host presents to the model?
options: Merge both tool definitions into one entry and forward every call to whichever server answers first
Prefix each tool name with a server identifier so the model can address search_docs and search_tickets without ambiguity
Reject both servers entirely at discovery time until their two separate authors formally agree on one single shared tool name
Silently keep only the first search tool discovered and drop the second one from the registry
questions.explanation: Because serverInfo.name is not guaranteed unique and tool names only need to be unique within one server, an aggregator that fronts multiple servers should prefix names to disambiguate. Dropping, merging, or racing servers all lose information the model needs to call the right tool.

questions.objective: Read the schemas and structured data that define MCP messages, tool definitions, capabilities, and server manifests
questions.prompt: A public-facing tool accepts a free-form object with no declared properties and additionalProperties left unset, versus an alternative design that lists each accepted field and sets additionalProperties to false. Which design better protects the tool and why?
options: Neither matters very much at all, since inputSchema is only ever shown to a human reviewer and never actually enforced anywhere by any code
The free-form schema, since it lets any future client send new fields without a schema update
The explicit schema, since it gives the server a precise contract and surfaces unexpected fields as feedback the model can act on
The free-form schema, since MCP requires every tool to accept arbitrary extra arguments for compatibility
questions.explanation: A tool's inputSchema is a real contract that the server validates arguments against, and a precise schema with additionalProperties false catches malformed or unexpected input early, returning it as a tool execution error the model can correct. An unconstrained schema defers that discovery to runtime logic instead.

questions.objective: Trace the model interaction flow from a user request through the host, model, client, and server and back into model context
questions.prompt: A team debates whether the confirm-before-destructive-action gate should live inside the server's tool implementation or inside the host, ahead of sending tools/call, given that annotations like destructiveHint are hints and untrusted unless the server itself is trusted. Where should the gate live?
options: Split randomly and unpredictably between host and server so a bypass in one place is unlikely to matter much
Inside the server, since only the server can be trusted to decide when to ask the user
Nowhere at all, since a genuinely well written tool description already makes an explicit confirmation step entirely unnecessary
Inside the host, since it can apply its own judgment and cannot rely on an untrusted server's hints
questions.explanation: Because annotations are hints the client must treat as untrusted unless the server is known trustworthy, the host cannot safely delegate the decision to confirm a destructive call to the server itself. The host is the place positioned to show inputs and gate the call before it is sent.

questions.objective: Distinguish the responsibilities of MCP hosts, clients, and servers and how discovery and capability negotiation connect them
questions.prompt: Which two statements correctly describe how discovery and capability negotiation connect an MCP host to a server? Select two.
options: A server must not rely on a capability the client did not declare on that request, and it errors naming what is missing
Once a client has successfully called server/discover one time, every later request on that same connection is exempt from repeating clientCapabilities
Calling server/discover is mandatory for every server to implement, though a client may skip it and send a request directly
Capability negotiation only applies to client capabilities and never constrains what a server is allowed to assume about itself
questions.explanation: Servers must implement server/discover even though calling it is optional for clients, and a server that needs an undeclared capability must reject the request rather than assume it, using the missing-capability error. Neither rule is relaxed by an earlier successful discovery on the same connection.

questions.objective: Read the schemas and structured data that define MCP messages, tool definitions, capabilities, and server manifests
questions.prompt: A tool author is deciding whether to add an outputSchema and return structuredContent, or keep returning only a text content block. When is adding outputSchema and structuredContent worth the extra design effort?
options: When downstream code must consume the result programmatically, since structuredContent should still be mirrored into a text block for older clients
Only when the server wants to drop stdio support and force clients onto Streamable HTTP
Only for those particular tools that take absolutely no arguments at all, since arguments and their outputs must always share exactly one single schema
Never, since only image and audio content blocks are ever permitted to appear alongside any structuredContent value at all
questions.explanation: structuredContent is valuable exactly when something downstream, a script or another tool, needs to parse the result reliably rather than a human reading prose. Because it must conform to outputSchema and should still be serialized into a text block, it adds a machine-readable contract without breaking older clients.

questions.objective: Trace the model interaction flow from a user request through the host, model, client, and server and back into model context
questions.prompt: After a tool call fails because an argument had the wrong date format, the host has two options: silently retry the exact same call, or feed the isError result's content back into the model's context. Which is the correct design and why?
options: Escalate every tool execution error straight to a human without giving the model a chance to respond
Feed the tool execution error back to the model, since that lets it read the content and self correct
Discard the failed call entirely and never mention it at all to either the model or the end user
Silently retry unchanged, since repeating the same call with the same arguments will eventually succeed
questions.explanation: Tool execution errors carry explanatory content precisely so the model can read what went wrong and adjust, which is the SEP-1303 rationale for treating input validation failures as results rather than opaque protocol errors. Retrying identical arguments blindly cannot fix a formatting mistake the model has not seen.

questions.objective: Read the schemas and structured data that define MCP messages, tool definitions, capabilities, and server manifests
questions.prompt: A manifest reviewer sees a tool definition that omits its annotations object entirely. Under the 2026-07-28 default values, how should the reviewer treat that tool when deciding whether the host needs a confirmation gate?
options: As read-only and safe, since omitting annotations means the server asserts the tool has no side effects
As idempotent by default in every case, since idempotentHint always defaults to true whenever a tool omits its annotations
As destructive by default, since destructiveHint defaults to true and openWorldHint defaults to true when omitted
As unknown, requiring the server's documentation before any confirmation policy can be set at all
questions.explanation: When annotations are omitted, the specification's defaults apply: readOnlyHint and idempotentHint default to false, while destructiveHint defaults to true and is only meaningful when the tool is not read only. A careful reviewer should treat an undeclared tool as potentially destructive rather than assuming safety.

questions.objective: Apply the request, notification, subscription, and multi round-trip interaction patterns and handle each result type
questions.prompt: A client library reuses the original JSON-RPC id when it retries a tools/call after answering an input_required result, reasoning that it is still logically the same call. Why does 2026-07-28 require a new id instead?
options: Because the client must close the connection between the original call and its retry attempt
Because ids are case sensitive strings, and reusing one would corrupt the transport framing layer
Because servers will always flatly refuse any id that has ever once been used before, even quite long after a response finally arrived
Because an id must not repeat one still awaiting a response, and the retry is a distinct request with inputResponses
questions.explanation: A request id must not be reused while still awaiting a response, and the MRTR retry is a new request that adds inputResponses and echoes requestState, not a continuation of the original one. Treating the retry as a fresh request with a new id keeps in-flight tracking correct.

questions.objective: Apply the request, notification, subscription, and multi round-trip interaction patterns and handle each result type
questions.prompt: A client stores an input_required result's requestState, then reformats its whitespace before echoing it back on retry because the two values look semantically equal. What goes wrong with this design if the server protects requestState with an HMAC?
options: The reformatted bytes no longer match what the HMAC was computed over, so the server rejects the retry as tampered
Nothing, since JSON-RPC guarantees semantically equal payloads always hash to the exact same value
The retry gets treated as a brand new tool call entirely unrelated to the original request
The server would always fall back immediately to the deprecated Dynamic Client Registration flow just to verify that one pending state
questions.explanation: requestState is meant to be echoed exactly, and an HMAC or AEAD is computed over the original bytes, so any reformatting, even whitespace only, changes what the server verifies against. Treating it as opaque and echoing it unmodified is the only design that keeps the integrity check meaningful.

lessons.title: The MCPA Blueprint Is a Study Budget, Not a Checklist
lessons.docsMarkdown:
# The MCPA Blueprint Is a Study Budget, Not a Checklist

> A syllabus lists what might appear on an exam. A blueprint states how often each part actually does. Read the MCPA blueprint as a budget for your study hours, not a table of contents to skim once and forget.

**Type:** Orientation
**Languages:** Python
**Prerequisites:** None
**Time:** ~45 minutes

## Learning Objectives

- Name the five MCPA domains and their exact published weights, and confirm they total 100 percent
- Convert a domain's blueprint weight into a proportional share of a fixed study-hours budget
- State the MCPA exam's format, fee, validity period, and retake policy, and reconcile the certification page's 90 minute duration against the launch press release's conflicting 120 minute figure
- Explain why the exam's item count and passing score are not published, and what that means for how a candidate calibrates readiness
- Read an exam question for a legacy-era distractor, such as an `initialize` handshake, a session, or `-32601` for an unknown tool, and reason to the 2026-07-28 replacement
- Trace the 34-lesson route from this orientation lesson through the capstone, and say which domain, or domains, each lesson belongs to

## The Problem

The Model Context Protocol touches a lot of surface area: roles and messages, schemas, transports, tool and resource lifecycles, sampling, error handling, OAuth, consent, auditability, and the ecosystem that has grown up around all of it. A candidate who opens the MCPA guide and starts reading top to bottom, spending roughly equal time on every topic, is making a study-plan decision without realizing it: that every part of the syllabus matters equally. It does not. The certification page that defines this exam also publishes a blueprint, a breakdown of five domains with a percentage weight attached to each one. That number is not decoration. It is the closest thing to an answer key the provider gives you before exam day, because it states how the exam's content is distributed across domains, on average.

Ignoring the blueprint is a planning bug, the same kind of bug as building a cache that never gets invalidated: it looks fine until the mismatch between assumption and reality costs you. Spend your hours evenly across five domains and you will, by construction, under-study the domain worth 26 percent of the exam and over-study the one worth 14 percent. The gap compounds because two domains, Interactions and Execution and Security and Governance, together account for half the blueprint. A study plan that does not know this treats a domain that is nearly twice as heavy as another as though they were interchangeable.

There is a third problem, and it costs points rather than hours. Every MCPA question is written against the 2026-07-28 release, but a candidate's intuition about MCP is often shaped by older tutorials, blog posts, and even earlier drafts of this curriculum, all describing a protocol that opened every connection with an `initialize` handshake and kept state in a session. An option that describes that older protocol reads as familiar, even authoritative, and familiarity is exactly what makes it a convincing wrong answer. A candidate who cannot tell a legacy-era belief from a 2026-07-28 fact on sight will lose points to options that sound right for the wrong reason. Finally, a 34-lesson curriculum is easy to read start to finish without ever noticing which of the five domains a given lesson is training. This lesson exists to fix all four problems before you read another lesson in this track: turn the published weights into an explicit hours budget, build a readiness signal that is honest about what the guide does and does not tell you, train the reflex that catches a legacy-era distractor, and hand you the route that maps all 34 lessons onto the five domains they build toward.

## The Concept

Start with the numbers themselves, because they are the whole foundation of the plan. The MCPA blueprint publishes five domains: MCP Fundamentals at 16 percent, Architecture and Components at 14 percent, Interactions and Execution at 26 percent, Security and Governance at 24 percent, and Use Cases and Ecosystem at 20 percent. Add them and you get exactly 100, which is worth checking yourself rather than trusting a summary, because a blueprint that does not sum to 100 is a sign something was transcribed wrong. Each domain also publishes named sub-competencies. MCP Fundamentals covers purpose and scope, core concepts, and interoperability and value. Architecture and Components covers schemas and structured data, the host, client, and server roles, and the model interaction flow. Interactions and Execution, the heaviest domain, covers interaction patterns and response handling, error handling, the tool invocation lifecycle, and protocol primitives. Security and Governance covers trust boundaries, permissions and consent, risk and safety controls, and auditability and observability. Use Cases and Ecosystem covers roles and adoption, operational use cases, and ecosystem portability. Every fact in this paragraph, along with its source and retrieval date, is recorded in `certifications/mcpa/research/source-verification-ledger.md` in this repository, so you can verify it yourself rather than take a lesson's word for it.

Next, the mechanics around the blueprint. The exam is delivered online, proctored, and multiple choice, and its content is aligned to the Model Context Protocol specification dated 2026-07-28, the same version this entire curriculum targets. The fee is 250 US dollars for the exam alone, separate from any bundled subscription. The credential is valid for two years, and a candidate who does not pass on the first attempt gets one included retake. Even the duration is not one clean number: the certification page itself states a 90 minute duration, while the Linux Foundation's own launch press release states 120 minutes. This curriculum follows the certification page, the exam-specific source, and records the press release's figure as an unresolved discrepancy rather than quietly picking whichever number looked more convenient; `certifications/mcpa/research/source-verification-ledger.md` carries both numbers with both sources so you can reverify before relying on either one. Two numbers are conspicuously absent from both sources: the exact number of items on the exam, and the passing score. Treat that absence as a fact in its own right, not a gap to paper over with a guess. It means your calibration target cannot be "answer at least N of 60 questions correctly." It has to be "reach solid, evenly distributed competence across all five domains," because that is the only target the published information actually supports.

Now connect the numbers to a plan. If a blueprint weight is a percentage of exam content, then the same percentage applied to a study-hours budget gives you a defensible per-domain target: hours for a domain equal your total budget multiplied by that domain's weight, divided by 100. This is ordinary proportional allocation, the same arithmetic behind sizing a budget line item or a portfolio position, and it is deterministic: the same budget and the same blueprint always produce the same split. The second half of the plan is measuring where you stand. A readiness estimate that simply averages your practice accuracy across five domains treats a domain worth 14 percent the same as one worth 26 percent, which quietly lets strength in a light domain cover for weakness in a heavy one. A weighted readiness estimate multiplies each domain's practice accuracy by that domain's blueprint weight before summing, so the number you look at tracks the exam's own emphasis instead of a naive five-way split. Both computations, the budget allocation and the weighted readiness estimate, are implemented as small, deterministic functions in `code/main.py`, and the figure below turns the five weights into a picture you can compare against your own allocation.

### Reading a question: catching a legacy-era distractor

A well-written distractor is not random noise. The MCPA exam is aligned to 2026-07-28, but MCP has gone through five revisions, and the belief system of the first, 2024-11-05, release is still everywhere: in old blog posts, in cached documentation, in an earlier draft of this very curriculum before it was corrected. That older belief system reads as fluent and confident, which is what makes it dangerous as a wrong answer. Train a specific reflex instead of a vague sense of caution. First, notice any option that describes a setup step, a handshake, or a negotiation before the first real request; 2026-07-28 has none, every request carries its own protocol version and capabilities in `_meta`, so an `initialize` call, or a claim that the connection negotiates a version up front, is a legacy-era tell. Second, notice any option that leans on a session or a sticky connection to explain how a server remembers something across calls; 2026-07-28 is stateless, and cross-request state travels as an explicit, server-minted handle passed back as an ordinary argument, never as an implicit session. Third, check any error code against what it actually means: an unknown tool is `-32602`, not the tempting `-32601`, which is reserved for an unknown method, and an argument that fails a tool's schema is not a protocol error at all, it is a normal result with `isError: true` that the model can read and correct. `certifications/mcpa/research/mcp-2026-07-28-brief.md`, section 16, keeps a running table of these traps, each wrong belief paired with the 2026-07-28 fact that replaced it; read it once before your first practice set and again the night before the exam.

### The route: 34 lessons across five domains

This track has 34 lessons, numbered 00 through 33, and every one of them is tagged to at least one of the five blueprint domains. Most lessons belong to exactly one domain: the tools primitive belongs to Interactions and Execution, OAuth belongs to Security and Governance, and so on down the route. A few lessons sit at a genuine intersection and are tagged with two domains at once. JSON-RPC and Meta is tagged Fundamentals and Architecture because the message envelope it teaches is both a core concept and a piece of the architecture the exam separately asks about; Transports and HTTP Headers is tagged Interactions and Architecture for the same reason, one mechanism, two angles the exam can question it from. The capstone lesson at the end of the route, lesson 33, is tagged with all five domains on purpose, because it is the one exchange that has to exercise every domain's ideas in a single transcript. `code/main.py` in this lesson encodes that entire route as data, not prose, so a script, or you, can ask "which lessons train Security and Governance" and get an exact, checkable answer instead of a guess from memory.

```figure
mcpa-00-blueprint-weights
```

## Interactive Lab

Run the script below. It validates the domain weights and the 34-lesson route, then prints the exam facts exactly as the two official sources state them, including the 90 versus 120 minute duration conflict and the two fields that are deliberately `null` because neither source publishes them. It allocates a 40-hour example budget across the five domains and prints the result next to a sample readiness computation built from example practice scores, alongside a naive unweighted average of the same scores so you can see the two numbers diverge. Finally it prints the full route length and the lesson slugs `route_for_domain` returns for two sample domains, the same question the route section above answers in prose.

```bash
python3 code/main.py
```

Hold the printed allocation table next to the figure above. The tallest bars, Interactions and Execution and Security and Governance, should also be the largest numbers in your printed allocation, because both come from the same five weights. If you change the `total_hours` value passed to `allocate_study_hours` in `demo()` and rerun the script, every number in the table moves in place while the proportions between domains stay fixed, because the split is relative to the blueprint, not to any specific budget size. Try calling `main.route_for_domain("not-a-real-domain")` from a Python shell in the lesson directory and watch it refuse the request instead of silently returning an empty route.

## Practice Lab

Before you open the next lesson in this track, do three things with your own numbers instead of the example ones baked into the demo. First, decide how many hours you actually have between now and your exam date, then call `allocate_study_hours` with that number and write down the five domain targets somewhere you will see them again, such as the shipped cheat sheet below. Second, as you work through practice questions or the diagnostic assessment in this track, keep a running `(correct, total)` tally for each domain, and periodically call `estimate_readiness` with that tally. Watch what happens to the number as you fill in a domain you had previously left at zero attempts: it should move, because an unpracticed domain scores as zero in the estimate rather than being quietly excluded. Third, call `route_for_domain` for whichever domain your readiness estimate says is weakest, and read that exact list of lessons next, in order, instead of continuing straight down the numbered list out of habit. Repeat all three checks weekly. A plan you built once and never revisited is not a plan, it is a snapshot.

## Shipped Artifact

`outputs/mcpa-blueprint-cheatsheet.md` is the one-page reference this lesson produces: all five domains with their weights and published sub-competencies, the fixed exam facts including the page-versus-press duration conflict and the two facts that are explicitly unpublished, a short legacy-era distractor checklist, and the full 34-lesson route table with each lesson's domain. Print it, pin it, or keep it open in a second window for the rest of this track.

## Verify It

Run the tests with `python3 -m unittest discover code/tests`. They check that the five domain weights sum to exactly 100 and that the validation guard rejects a weight set that does not, that a study-hours budget is split in exact proportion to those weights and that the split sums back to the original budget, that a weighted readiness estimate rewards mastery of the heaviest domain more than mastery of a lighter one rather than treating every domain the same, that a zero-hour budget allocates zero to every domain without special-casing, that a domain with no attempted practice questions contributes zero to readiness instead of raising a division error, that an unrecognized domain name is rejected by both the readiness estimate and the route lookup instead of failing silently, and that the route covers all 34 lessons numbered 00 through 33 with the capstone alone spanning every domain. If any of these fail, the code and this lesson have drifted apart, and the code is the source of truth for the arithmetic.

This lesson never exchanges a message with an MCP server, so its wire transcript is deliberately empty; the repository's wire checker confirms that the module explains why instead of silently shipping nothing:

```bash
python3 scripts/check_mcpa_wire.py certifications/mcpa/lessons/00-mcp-exam-strategy
```

## Capstone Connection

The `estimate_readiness` function you just ran is not a throwaway demo. It is the same weighted scoring model lesson 33, the capstone readiness review, expects you to run again, this time against your real diagnostic or mock-exam domain breakdown, to decide whether you are actually ready to schedule the exam or whether a specific domain still needs another pass. Keep the cheat sheet, the two study functions, and the route table in this lesson close. Every one of the 34 lessons that follows slots into at least one of the five weighted domains named here, and the capstone is where you prove, with your own numbers run back through this same math, that your coverage matches the blueprint rather than your reading order.

## Key Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| Blueprint | The published table of the five MCPA domains and their percentage weights |
| Domain weight | The percentage of exam content a single domain represents, on average |
| Study-hours budget | The fixed number of hours available before exam day, split across domains by weight |
| Readiness estimate | A weighted average of practice accuracy across domains, using blueprint weights instead of a plain average |
| Unpublished fact | An exam detail, such as item count or passing score, that neither official source states |
| Legacy-era distractor | A wrong answer option that describes MCP as it worked before 2026-07-28, such as an `initialize` handshake or a session |
| Route | The mapping from each of the 34 lessons to the domain, or domains, it trains |

## Further Reading

- Model Context Protocol specification, version 2026-07-28, at https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28, the release this entire blueprint and curriculum are aligned to.
- `certifications/mcpa/research/mcp-2026-07-28-brief.md`, section 16, for the full table of legacy-era traps this lesson's reading strategy is built from.
- `phases/13-tools-and-protocols/06-mcp-fundamentals` in this repository, for the deep-dive lesson on the core concepts every domain in the blueprint builds on.
- MCPA certification page, https://training.linuxfoundation.org/certification/model-context-protocol-associate-mcpa/, the official guide this lesson's exam facts are drawn from.
- `certifications/mcpa/research/source-verification-ledger.md` in this repository, for every fact above, including the duration discrepancy, with its source and retrieval date.

quiz.question: What does a domain's weight in the MCPA blueprint most directly tell a candidate?
options: The order in which the five domains appear in the official guide
The share of exam questions drawn from that domain, on average
The minimum score a candidate must reach in that domain alone
The number of official training hours required before attempting it
quiz.explanation: A domain's published weight is its share of the blueprint, the proportion of exam content the domain represents; it does not set a reading order, a required hour count, or a per-domain minimum score.

quiz.question: Which pair of domains carries the largest combined share of the MCPA blueprint?
options: MCP Fundamentals and Architecture and Components, the two foundational domains
Architecture and Components and Use Cases and Ecosystem, the two mid-weight domains
Interactions and Execution and Security and Governance, the two heaviest domains
Use Cases and Ecosystem and MCP Fundamentals, the two adoption-facing domains
quiz.explanation: Interactions and Execution is weighted 26 percent and Security and Governance is weighted 24 percent, together half the blueprint, which is why they deserve the largest share of study hours.

quiz.question: The MCPA certification page and the Linux Foundation's own launch press release disagree about one exam fact. Which fact is it, and which source does this curriculum follow?
options: The included retake count
The credential validity period
The exam fee
The exam duration
quiz.explanation: The certification page states a 90 minute duration while the press release states 120 minutes; this curriculum follows the certification page as the exam-specific source and records the conflict rather than silently choosing a number.

quiz.question: A practice question claims a client must call initialize before a 2026-07-28 server will accept any other request. How should a prepared candidate read that claim?
options: A legacy-era protocol distractor
True only for older MCP servers
A detail specific to stdio only
A true, still current requirement
quiz.explanation: The 2026-07-28 revision removed the initialize handshake and protocol sessions entirely, so every request now carries its own protocol version and capabilities in its metadata instead of relying on a prior handshake.

quiz.question: A candidate scores 100 percent in MCP Fundamentals, weighted 16 percent, and 0 percent everywhere else. Why is a weighted readiness estimate more useful here than a plain five-way average?
options: It rounds every domain score upward so the candidate always looks prepared
It shows readiness near 16 percent instead of a misleading 20 percent average
It replaces the five domains with a single combined pass or fail flag
It discards the weakest domain scores before computing any final result
quiz.explanation: A plain average shows 20 percent because one of five domains is perfect, but a weighted estimate reflects that the mastered domain is only 16 percent of the exam, which is a more honest picture of overall readiness.

quiz.question: A few lessons in the 34-lesson route, such as JSON-RPC and Meta, are tagged with two domains instead of one. What does that reflect about the route?
options: A sign those lessons are optional to skip

lessons.title: Reading the MCP Specification
lessons.docsMarkdown:
# Reading the MCP Specification

> The specification is normative text, not a tutorial: a MUST decides an implementation, a SHOULD leaves room for judgment, and a feature's Deprecated state tells you exactly how long you can still rely on it.

**Type:** Reference
**Languages:** Python
**Prerequisites:** Lesson 00
**Time:** ~45 minutes

## Learning Objectives

- Navigate the specification's structure: which parts every implementation MUST support and which are added as needed
- Read RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 keyword strength correctly, including the rule that lowercase words carry no normative weight
- Explain the relationship between schema.ts and schema.json, and why the TypeScript file is the source of truth
- Tell a Draft, Current, or Final revision apart from a feature's own Active, Deprecated, or Removed state
- Trace a changelog entry back to the SEP that produced it, and compute a Deprecated feature's earliest removal from its window

## The Problem

Every fact in this curriculum traces back to one document: the specification at modelcontextprotocol.io, built from a TypeScript schema. A team that learns MCP from a blog post, from a training run whose data predates the current revision, or from memory of an earlier release drifts away from what the specification actually requires, and the exam is written against the specification, not against what used to be true. An implementation that remembered the 2025-06-18 revision correctly and never reread the current text would still get 2026-07-28 wrong, because a MUST from an older revision can be replaced by a different rule, and a feature that used to sit at the center of the protocol can move to Deprecated with a migration path attached while continuing to work exactly as before.

Reading the specification is a skill in its own right: knowing where the normative text lives, what its keywords actually commit an implementation to, how a document's own maturity differs from an individual feature's state, and how to trace a claim back to the proposal that produced it instead of trusting a summary.

## The Concept

The specification is organized into a small number of parts: architecture, the base protocol, versioning and compatibility, message patterns, authorization, server features, client features, and utilities, with optional extensions layered on top. The overview page states plainly which of these are mandatory: all implementations MUST support the base protocol, versioning, and the message patterns. Everything else, including authorization, server features, client features, and utilities, MAY be implemented based on what the application actually needs. That single sentence is worth remembering on its own, because it marks the floor: a server with no resources and no prompts, offering only tools over stdio with no authorization at all, is still a conformant MCP server, as long as it gets the base protocol, versioning, and message patterns right.

Every message shape in this curriculum, and every message shape the exam can ask about, ultimately comes from one file: schema.ts, the TypeScript schema in the specification repository. The prose pages are a readable explanation of that schema, not an independent source of truth; where prose and schema seem to disagree, schema.ts wins. schema.json is generated automatically from schema.ts for tooling that cannot parse TypeScript, and it carries no authority of its own. When a question turns on the exact shape of a result or an error, the schema is where the answer actually lives.

The specification's normative language follows BCP 14, the combination of RFC 2119 and RFC 8174: the words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, NOT RECOMMENDED, MAY, and OPTIONAL carry their defined strength only when they appear in all capitals, exactly as shown here. A sentence that says a client must not batch requests, written in lowercase, is ordinary prose with no normative force at all; the identical words as MUST NOT are a hard prohibition. Reading strength correctly means noticing case, not just vocabulary. MUST and MUST NOT set a floor an implementation cannot go under. SHOULD and SHOULD NOT describe a strong default that a specific, understood reason can override. MAY and OPTIONAL describe a real choice with no default either way.

A specification revision, the whole dated document, is in one of three states. Draft revisions are in progress and not ready for consumption. Current is the one revision in active use; 2026-07-28 is Current today, and it may still receive backwards-compatible changes. The identifier itself is a date in YYYY-MM-DD form that marks the last day backwards incompatible changes were made, which is why a Current revision can absorb compatible fixes without being renamed. Final revisions are past and complete; they will not change again. Because the protocol is stateless, a client that wants to know which revision a server actually speaks does not have to guess from documentation: it can call server/discover, the specification's entry point, and read the answer back on the wire.

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "method": "server/discover",
  "params": {
    "_meta": {
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28",
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {}
    }
  }
}
```

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "result": {
    "resultType": "complete",
    "supportedVersions": ["2026-07-28"],
    "capabilities": {"tools": {"listChanged": false}},
    "ttlMs": 300000,
    "cacheScope": "public"
  }
}
```

A feature inside a Current revision, one message, one capability, one transport, carries its own state, separate from the revision's Draft, Current, or Final label. Active means implement it as written, with no planned removal. Deprecated means the feature is still fully specified and functional, but a migration path is documented and the feature is scheduled to go away; new implementations should not adopt it. Removed means it has been deleted from the draft specification and will not appear in the next Current revision. Roots, Sampling, Logging, and Dynamic Client Registration are all Deprecated in 2026-07-28, not removed: they still work exactly as specified, and a server or client that supports them today keeps working tomorrow. The deprecated features registry is the single page that lists every feature currently in the Deprecated or Removed state, so a reader never has to reconstruct that picture from scattered changelog entries.

The deprecation policy sets a floor, not a fixed schedule. A feature must remain Deprecated for at least twelve months before it is even eligible for removal, and that window is measured from the release of the revision that first marks it Deprecated, not from whenever the proposal that deprecated it happened to reach Final. The date the window elapses is the feature's earliest removal, the first Current revision released on or after that point; whether the feature is actually removed in that revision, in a later one, or stays Deprecated far longer, is a Core Maintainer decision made during release preparation. Because Roots, Sampling, Logging, and Dynamic Client Registration were all marked Deprecated in the revision released on 2026-07-28, their shared earliest removal is the first revision released on or after 2027-07-28, computed from that release date rather than from any single proposal's own timeline.

Every substantial change to the specification, a new feature, a breaking change, a governance change, goes through a Specification Enhancement Proposal: a markdown file in the seps directory that states the motivation, the exact specification text, the rationale, backward compatibility, and security implications. A SEP moves through draft and in-review status and is either accepted or rejected, and it only reaches final once a reference implementation and, for standards-track changes with observable behavior, a conformance scenario both exist. An Extensions Track SEP follows the identical process but describes an optional extension rather than a core protocol addition. Every changelog entry in the specification names the SEP that produced it; reading that SEP is how a careful implementer, or a careful exam candidate, confirms a claim instead of trusting a one-line summary. The feature lifecycle and deprecation policy itself, the rule this lesson leans on for Active, Deprecated, and Removed, is SEP-2596, a Process SEP that reached Final status by documenting exactly the mechanism described above.

JSON-RPC batching is the cautionary example the lifecycle policy was written to prevent: it was added in the revision released on 2025-03-26 and removed one release later, on 2025-06-18, with no deprecation period at all. Under 2026-07-28, that kind of change is not supposed to happen again without at least a twelve-month Deprecated state and a documented migration path first.

```figure
mcpa-01-spec-map
```

## Interactive Lab

The figure maps the specification around a single root: three boxes marked MUST support the base protocol, versioning, and message patterns, and four boxes marked MAY support authorization, server features, client features, and utilities. Below it, three chips trace a feature's own lifecycle, Active to Deprecated to Removed, a state that travels with the feature, not with the revision. A box can be MUST while everything under it, including exactly which tools or resources a given server chooses to expose, remains entirely up to the implementation.

## Practice Lab

Open `code/main.py`. It has no network calls and models the specification as data rather than talking to a real server: a deprecated features registry, a small changelog indexed by SEP number, and a keyword classifier.

```bash
python3 code/main.py
```

Read the printed output against the concept section above. `classify_requirement` reads a sentence and returns its strength, and shows that the identical words written in lowercase return `unspecified` rather than `forbidden`. `feature_state` answers whether roots, sampling, or JSON-RPC batching count as active, deprecated, or removed as of a given revision, and `earliest_removal` computes the 2027-07-28 date directly from the deprecation window instead of having it hardcoded anywhere. `changelog_lookup` takes a SEP number and returns the entry that cites it. At the end, the demo sends a `server/discover` request and prints the exchange, along with something that goes wrong on purpose: a request missing its required `_meta` block, which a conformant server must reject rather than guess about. Add a new entry to `DEPRECATED_REGISTRY` with its own window, or change which feature `include-context-this-server-all-servers` follows, and rerun to see `earliest_removal` and `feature_state` pick up the change without any other code moving.

## Shipped Artifact

`outputs/spec-reading-guide.md` is a one-page reference you can keep open while reading the actual specification: the MUST-support list, the keyword strength table, the difference between a revision's state and a feature's state, and the deprecation timing rules with their exact anchor points. Use it as a checklist before you tell a teammate, or answer an exam question, about whether something is still current.

## Verify It

Run the tests from the lesson directory:

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover code/tests
```

They check the claims in this lesson: MUST and MUST NOT classify as required and forbidden, the identical lowercase words classify as unspecified, SHOULD and MAY classify as recommended and optional, SHOULD NOT and NOT RECOMMENDED both classify as not recommended, a feature is active before its own deprecation revision and deprecated on or after it, a feature that only has a removal date and no Deprecated state at all is never reported as current, earliest removal is computed from the twelve-month window rather than hardcoded, a feature that follows another feature's schedule shares its earliest removal, an unrecognized feature name is handled without raising, a changelog entry can be found by its SEP number while an unknown SEP returns nothing, and a queried revision correctly reports Current, Final, or unknown. The repository's wire checker also validates the lesson's transcript against the 2026-07-28 rules:

```bash
python3 scripts/check_mcpa_wire.py certifications/mcpa/lessons/01-reading-the-specification
```

## Capstone Connection

The capstone assembles one full 2026-07-28 exchange end to end, and it assumes you can tell, without looking anything up, whether a message shape, an error code, or a feature it uses is still current. Every later lesson in this track cites a specific page or SEP the way this one taught you to read them: by keyword strength, by feature state, and by the SEP that actually produced the rule. When the capstone, or an exam question, rests on whether something is a MUST or a SHOULD, or whether a feature is Deprecated rather than Removed, you are reading the same registry and the same keywords this lesson modeled as data.

## Key Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| Base protocol | The JSON-RPC message shapes every implementation MUST support |
| BCP 14 | The RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 rule that MUST, SHOULD, and MAY carry normative weight only in all capitals |
| schema.ts | The TypeScript file that is the source of truth for every MCP message and structure |
| Current revision | The one specification revision in active use; 2026-07-28 today |
| Draft, Current, Final | The three states a specification revision moves through |
| Active | A feature's state when it is implemented per its normative requirements with no planned removal |
| Deprecated | A feature's state when it is still specified and functional but scheduled for removal with a migration path |
| Removed | A feature's state once it has been deleted from the draft specification |
| Earliest removal | The first Current revision released on or after a Deprecated feature's minimum window elapses |
| SEP | A Specification Enhancement Proposal, the markdown document that proposes and records a specification change |

## Further Reading

- [MCP specification 2026-07-28](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28)
- [MCP specification 2026-07-28, Base Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic)
- [MCP specification 2026-07-28, Changelog](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog)
- [MCP specification 2026-07-28, Deprecated Features](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/deprecated)
- [Feature Lifecycle and Deprecation Policy](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/community/feature-lifecycle)
- [SEP Guidelines](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/community/sep-guidelines)
- `certifications/mcpa/research/mcp-2026-07-28-brief.md`, sections 1 and 15
- `phases/13-tools-and-protocols/31-mcp-conformance-versioning-and-operations`, which builds a conformance harness on top of these version-era rules

quiz.question: According to the specification overview, which three components MUST every MCP implementation support?
options: Server features, client features, and utilities
Resources, prompts, tools, and elicitation together
The base protocol, versioning, and message patterns
Authorization, extensions, and completion utilities
quiz.explanation: The specification states that all implementations MUST support the base protocol, versioning, and the message patterns, while server features, client features, authorization, and utilities MAY be implemented as the application needs them.

quiz.question: A sentence reads, written in lowercase, that a client must not batch requests. What normative weight does that carry under BCP 14?
options: The same forbidding weight as MUST NOT written in capitals
It makes that whole paragraph an invalid specification page
A soft recommendation, treated the same as SHOULD NOT
No normative weight; only capitalized keywords count
quiz.explanation: BCP 14 keywords carry their defined meaning only when they appear in all capitals; the identical words in lowercase are ordinary prose with no normative force.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between schema.ts and schema.json in the specification repository?
options: schema.ts is the source of truth and schema.json is generated from it
schema.json is authoritative for SDKs and schema.ts is only a draft
schema.json is written by hand first and schema.ts is generated from it
The two files are maintained independently and are free to disagree
quiz.explanation: The specification names schema.ts the source of truth for every protocol message and structure, with schema.json generated automatically from it for tooling.

quiz.question: A feature is marked Deprecated in the specification revision released on 2026-07-28 with a twelve-month window. From what point is that window measured?
options: From the day the Core Maintainers approved the SEP in review
From the release of the specification revision that marks it Deprecated
From the day the deprecation SEP itself reached Final status
From the day the deprecation SEP was first opened as a pull request
quiz.explanation: SEP-2596 measures the deprecation window from the release of the revision that first marks the feature Deprecated, not from whenever its own SEP happened to reach Final.

quiz.question: Roots, Sampling, and Logging are sometimes described as having been removed in the 2026-07-28 revision. What does the specification actually say about their state?
options: Active still; nothing about their status changed in this revision
Removed outright; a conformant server MUST NOT implement them
Deprecated, not removed; still fully specified and functional
Experimental now; only Tier 3 SDKs are required to support them
quiz.explanation: SEP-2577 deprecated Roots, Sampling, and Logging in the 2026-07-28 revision; they remain fully specified and functional, with removal not eligible before the first revision released on or after 2027-07-28.

quiz.question: A changelog entry cites a SEP number as the source of a major protocol change. What should a careful reader do before repeating that claim?
options: Assume the change is still in review until the next revision ships
Read only the schema.json diff, since SEPs rarely touch the schema
Trust the one-line changelog summary, since SEPs close once accepted
Open the SEP file for its text, rationale, and final status
quiz.explanation: A changelog entry links back to the SEP that produced it, and reading the SEP itself confirms the exact specification text, the rationale, and whether it actually reached Final status.

lessons.title: The Integration Problem MCP Solves
lessons.docsMarkdown:
# The Integration Problem MCP Solves

> Every system you connect to an AI application is a contract. MCP makes that contract the same shape everywhere, so one client can use a server it has never seen before.

**Type:** Reference
**Languages:** Python
**Prerequisites:** Lesson 01
**Time:** ~45 minutes

## Learning Objectives

- Explain the N times M integration problem and how one shared protocol reduces it to N plus M
- State what MCP standardizes between AI applications and external systems, and what it deliberately leaves out
- Name the participants of an MCP system and the three server primitives in one sentence each
- Read a discovery request, a tool list, and a tool call as ordinary JSON-RPC messages carrying per-request metadata
- Tell a protocol error from a tool execution error and explain why the difference matters to the model

## The Problem

Connecting an AI application to an outside system used to mean writing glue. An assistant that needed your files, your ticket queue, and your database needed three integrations, and each one invented its own way to describe what it could do, its own argument format, its own error shape, and its own idea of who was allowed to call it. A fourth system meant a fourth integration. A second AI application meant writing all of them again, because nothing written for the first one fit the second.

That is an N times M problem. Four applications and six systems cost twenty-four integrations, and every one of them is a place where the format drifts and the security assumptions blur. The expensive part is not the first integration. It is the twentieth, and the review that has to reason about all twenty at once.

The Model Context Protocol turns N times M into N plus M. Each application learns to speak MCP once. Each system exposes an MCP server once. Any modern client can then use any modern server, because both sides agree on one message format, one way to describe capabilities, and one way to call a tool and read what comes back. Four applications and six systems now cost ten implementations, and each new system adds one.

## The Concept

MCP is a protocol, not a product. It standardizes the conversation between an AI application and the systems that give it context and let it act: how a server describes itself, how a client asks what the server offers, how a tool is invoked, and how results and errors come back. It deliberately does not standardize the model, which model a host uses, how the host builds its prompt, or what the user interface looks like. Those stay the application's decisions.

The participants are few. The **host** is the application the user works in, such as a chat assistant or an editor. Inside the host, a **client** manages the conversation with one **server**, and a host runs one client per server it uses. A server exposes three kinds of **primitives**. **Tools** are named, described, schema-typed actions the model can decide to invoke. **Resources** are readable data, identified by URIs, that the application chooses to place in context. **Prompts** are reusable templates the user picks explicitly. Who is in control differs for each: tools are model-controlled, resources are application-driven, and prompts are user-controlled.

Every message is JSON-RPC 2.0. A request has an `id`, a `method`, and `params`. A response carries either a `result` or an `error` with the same `id`. In the 2026-07-28 revision, the one the MCPA exam is aligned to, every request also carries its own protocol metadata in `params._meta`: the protocol version under the key `io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion`, the client's capabilities under `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities`, and, recommended, the client's name and version under `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo`. There is no opening handshake and no session. Each request stands on its own, which is why any replica of a server can answer it.

Every result carries a `resultType`. For now you will see `complete`, meaning the result holds the final content. Later lessons introduce `input_required`, the answer a server gives when it needs something from the user before it can finish.

Discovery is data, not code. A client can call `server/discover` to learn which protocol versions a server supports, which capabilities it offers, and its name, and it can call `tools/list` to receive each tool's name, description, and input schema. Nothing is compiled into the client ahead of time. That is the entire interoperability argument in one sentence: a client written today can drive a server written next year, because the server describes itself in the protocol.

Errors come in two kinds, and the exam cares about the difference.
